introduction: The guide asks its reader to stop taking the visible world for the whole of existence. It speaks of worlds without number, of the realms of God, of Command and of creation, of the kingdoms of mineral, plant, animal and human being, and of this life as a womb for the next. Its ninety-seven quotations are read here with ninety-seven from elsewhere. Scripture supplies the oldest forms of the same widening: the Lord of the Worlds, the heaven of heavens that cannot contain God, Jacob’s ladder, the third heaven, the many mansions. Plato’s cave and his Good beyond being, Aristotle’s unmoved mover, Plotinus’s overflowing One and Lao Tzu’s Tao are the philosophers’ maps of the same ascent, and Pope, Milton, Dante, Wordsworth and Rumi give the poets’. Other voices doubt the journey or redirect it: Lucretius, for whom nothing waits; Pascal, frightened by the silence of infinite space; Arnold on his darkling plain; Blake and Khayyam, who find heaven here or within. They are set where the guide itself answers the denier, so that its answer can be weighed.
questions: The guide says the worlds of God are countless and yet a single world with many stations. Which of the outside pictures (a ladder, a chain, a cave, an overflowing source) helps you most to hold those two statements together?
The denier asks where that other world is. How do Paul, Hamlet and Emily Dickinson each answer, and how does the guide?
Pascal is frightened by infinite space and the psalmist is moved to praise by the heavens. What makes the difference between their two responses?
The guide compares this life to the womb. What would it change in a day's conduct to take that comparison seriously?
Blake sees heaven in a wild flower and Khayyam finds heaven and hell within himself. Are these rivals to the guide's many worlds, or other ways of saying it?
Several readings place the human being between the animal and the divine. What does each realm ask of us while we stand in between?

outside.why: The opening chapter of the Qur'an praises God as Lord of the Worlds, in the plural, before it asks for anything.
Hebrews also speaks of worlds in the plural, framed by the word of God, the seen not made of things which appear.
Paul gives the same direction to the affections: seek the things that are above, and set the mind there and not on the earth.
Hamlet's answer to a sceptical friend is that heaven and earth hold more things than his philosophy has dreamt of.
Paul reverses the denier's test of reality: the things which are seen are temporal, and the things not seen are eternal.
Lucretius bids his reader look back on the time before birth, which was nothing to us, as a mirror of the time after death. What could be said to someone for whom that settles the matter?
Dickinson never saw a moor or the sea and yet knows how the heather looks, and is as certain of heaven. What kind of knowledge of an unseen place is that?
Asked when the kingdom of God should come, Jesus refuses 'lo here' and 'lo there': it is not a place to be pointed at.
After naming the animals people ride, the Qur'an adds simply that God creates that which you do not know.
Job calls everything he has described only parts of God's ways, and asks how little a portion of him is heard.
For Pascal the infinite spaces are silent, and their eternal silence frightens him. Why might countless worlds console one mind and terrify another?
The Qur'an names the same pair in a single phrase, creation and commandment, and says that both belong to the Lord of the Worlds.
Lao Tzu also counts downward from a source: the Tao produced One, One produced Two, Two produced Three, and Three all things.
Pope pictures the degrees as one vast chain of being which began from God and runs through angel, man, beast, bird, fish and insect.
Milton's angel tells Adam of various degrees of substance and of life, all proceeding from one Almighty and returning up to him.
The Qur'an gathers four names for God into a single line: the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward.
The Qur'an states it as a matter of sight: vision does not comprehend Him, but He comprehends all vision.
Isaiah measures the distance by the sky: as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are God's ways and thoughts higher than ours.
Solomon, speaking of the house he has built, admits that heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain the one it is built for.
At the bush the divine name given to Moses is being itself: I AM THAT I AM, and I AM hath sent me.
Plato's Timaeus says that the father and maker of all this universe is past finding out.
Paul speaks of one who is the image of the invisible God and the firstborn of every creature, standing between the two.
Jesus speaks as one who stands in another realm than his hearers: ye are from beneath, I am from above.
Spinoza holds that all things which are, are in God and depend on God. Is a third realm between God and creation needed, or does this already say enough?
Plotinus pictures the One, lacking nothing, as having overflowed, and its exuberance as producing something new.
Hebrews speaks of one who is the brightness of God's glory and the express image of his person, by whom the worlds were made.
Paul tells of a man caught up to the third heaven, who heard unspeakable words which it is not lawful for a man to utter.
Jacob's dream joins the realms by a ladder set up on the earth with its top in heaven, and angels ascending and descending on it.
The Qur'an counts seven heavens and of the earth the like, with the commandment coming down among them.
Dante begins his Paradise with a glory that penetrates the whole universe and shines in one part more and in another less.
Blake would see a world in a grain of sand and a heaven in a wild flower. Are the higher realms somewhere else, or a way of seeing this one?
Hebrews calls the earthly service an example and shadow of heavenly things, made according to a pattern shown on the mount.
Emerson's one sentence makes the lower world a language for the higher: every natural fact is a symbol of some spiritual fact.
The Qur'an pictures the ordinance directed from the heaven to the earth and ascending again in a day measured as a thousand years.
Plato sets above the visible world and the known a Good which, like the sun, is the author of what is beneath it.
Paul reasons in the same direction: the invisible things are clearly seen from the creation of the world.
Plato's prisoners have lived chained in an underground den from childhood, able to see only what is in front of them.
Plato describes the ascent as a turning of the whole soul, as an eye must turn with the whole body from darkness to light.
Wordsworth calls our birth a sleep and a forgetting, and the soul that rises with us our life's star.
Rumi tells the ascent as a series of deaths: dying as inanimate matter to rise a plant, and as a plant to rise an animal.
In the Phaedo the lovers of knowledge are conscious that the soul sees existence only through the bars of a prison.
Emerson, standing on the bare ground, feels uplifted into infinite space while all mean egotism vanishes. Is such a moment a glimpse of another realm or a mood of this one?
The Qur'an's answer about the Spirit is brief: it is by command of the Lord, and of knowledge little has been given.
Coleridge sings of the one Life within us and abroad, which meets all motion and becomes its soul.
Wordsworth has felt a presence deeply interfused in sun, ocean, air and the mind of man: a motion and a spirit.
Genesis tells of the breath of life breathed into the nostrils, by which man became a living soul.
The psalm makes every creature depend on that breath: the spirit is sent forth, they are created, and the face of the earth is renewed.
Aristotle observes that nature proceeds little by little from lifeless things to animal life, so that no exact line can be drawn.
Whitman calls himself an acme of things accomplished, with all the steps below duly travelled, and still mounting.
Thoreau asks whether he is not partly leaves and vegetable mould himself. Does kinship with the lower kingdoms lower the human being, or root it?
Dickinson measures the mental against the physical world: the brain is wider than the sky, for it will contain the other.
Paul distinguishes celestial bodies from terrestrial, and says the glory of the one is not the glory of the other.
Pascal places the human being between two others: neither angel nor brute, and unfortunate when trying to act the angel.
Pope's man is placed on an isthmus of a middle state, in doubt whether to deem himself a god or a beast.
Plato's image of the divided human being is a charioteer driving a pair, one of the horses noble and of noble breed.
The Preacher draws a practical lesson from the two estates: God is in heaven and thou upon earth, therefore let thy words be few.
Keats complains that cold philosophy makes charms fly and puts the rainbow in the dull catalogue of common things. Is a world narrowed to its matter a finding of science or a habit of mind?
Arnold's world only seems a land of dreams and has really neither joy nor light nor certitude. What can be said to someone for whom this is simply honest?
Keats knows the feeling of a horizon suddenly widened: a watcher of the skies when a new planet swims into his ken.
The saying quoted here comes from John's Gospel: in the Father's house are many mansions, and it would have been said if it were not so.
Isaiah's high and lofty One inhabits eternity, and dwells also with whoever is of a contrite and humble spirit.
Job goes forward and backward, to the left hand and the right, and still cannot perceive or behold him.
Paul quotes an older saying: eye has not seen, nor ear heard, what God has prepared for those who love him.
Isaiah uses the same scale for all the nations together: a drop of a bucket, the small dust of the balance.
Hebrews speaks of those who confessed themselves strangers and pilgrims on the earth. Is feeling confined in this world a sign of belonging elsewhere, or a temptation to neglect it?
The Preacher makes the womb the measure of our ignorance: we do not know how the bones grow there, nor the works of God.
Paul describes present knowledge as seeing through a glass, darkly, and what is to come as seeing face to face.
Seneca uses the image of birth as well: the day feared as the end of all things is the birthday of eternity.
John's letter admits that it does not yet appear what we shall be, only that we shall be like him.
Paul calls the body an earthly house that may be dissolved, and expects a house not made with hands, eternal in the heavens.
The Qur'an calls the life of this world a pastime and a game, and the home of the Hereafter the real life.
The Qur'an's prayer asks for what is good in the world and what is good in the Hereafter together. Does widening the horizon to other realms lessen the claim of this one?
The psalm gives such thirst its image: as the hart pants after the water brooks, so the soul thirsts for the living God.
Deuteronomy draws the line plainly: the secret things belong to the Lord, and the things revealed belong to us.
Kant's awe has two objects, the starry heavens above and the moral law within. Does wonder at what is seen and felt lead toward unseen realms, or take their place?
Paul prays that his friends may comprehend the breadth and length and depth and height, and know a love that passes knowledge.
Thoreau says that castles in the air are where they should be, and that foundations must now be put under them. What is the foundation under a flight toward the unseen?
Augustine's prayer has the same homesickness: made for God, our hearts are restless until they rest in him.
The Lord's Prayer asks that the kingdom come and the will be done in earth as it is in heaven.
The psalm hears the same call in creation: the heavens declare the glory of God and the firmament shows his handiwork.
The Throne Verse gives to one living God whatever is in the heavens and whatever is in the earth, whom neither slumber nor sleep overtakes.
The psalm divides the realms: the heavens are the Lord's, but the earth he has given to the children of men. Is this world ours to dwell in, or only to pass through?
Paul lists every power and realm he can name, height and depth among them, and says none can separate us from the love of God.
The psalmist, considering the heavens as the work of God's fingers, asks what man is that God is mindful of him.
Isaiah gives the same pair of images, heaven the throne and earth the footstool, and asks what house could be built for such a one.
Jesus says that his kingdom is not of this world, and that if it were his servants would fight.
Shelley's image of the two realms is life as a dome of many-coloured glass that stains the white radiance of eternity.
Plotinus compares what is produced from the Supreme to the brilliant light encircling the sun, generated from an unchanging substance.
Aristotle's highest reality is a divine thought which thinks of itself, so that its thinking is a thinking on thinking.
Lao Tzu begins with a warning: the Tao that can be trodden is not the enduring and unchanging Tao.
Krishna says in the Gita that all these things hang on him as a row of pearls hangs upon its string.
Aristotle's final cause produces motion as a thing that is loved does, while all other things move by being moved.
Dante is told of a single point that heaven and all nature are dependent on it.
Marcus Aurelius sees all things from eternity as of like forms, coming round in a circle. Is existence a ladder of kinds, or one round repeated?
The Gita pictures the spirit putting by its garb of flesh as one lays worn-out robes away, and passing to a residence afresh.
Arnold describes wandering between two worlds, one dead and the other powerless to be born. Can a person belong fully to neither realm?
Khayyam's soul, sent through the Invisible, returns to answer 'I myself am Heaven and Hell'. What is lost, and what gained, if the other worlds are within?

corinthians-caught-up-to-the-third-heave.text: I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago, (whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) such an one caught up to the third heaven. And I knew such a man, (whether in the body, or out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth;) How that he was caught up into paradise, and heard unspeakable words, which it is not lawful for a man to utter

psalm-when-i-consider-thy-heavens.text: When I consider thy heavens, the work of thy fingers, the moon and the stars, which thou hast ordained; What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him? For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and honour

luke-kingdom-of-god-is-within-you.text: And when he was demanded of the Pharisees, when the kingdom of God should come, he answered them and said, The kingdom of God cometh not with observation: Neither shall they say, Lo here! or, lo there! for, behold, the kingdom of God is within you

john-earthly-things-heavenly-things.text: If I have told you earthly things, and ye believe not, how shall ye believe, if I tell you of heavenly things

john-ye-are-from-beneath.text: And he said unto them, Ye are from beneath; I am from above: ye are of this world; I am not of this world

psalm-earth-given-to-the-children-of-men.text: The heaven, even the heavens, are the Lord's: but the earth hath he given to the children of men

quran-a-day-of-a-thousand-years.text: He directeth the ordinance from the heaven unto the earth; then it ascendeth unto Him in a Day, whereof the measure is a thousand years of that ye reckon.

quran-seven-heavens-and-of-the-earth.text: Allah it is who hath created seven heavens, and of the earth the like thereof. The commandment cometh down among them slowly, that ye may know that Allah is Able to do all things, and that Allah surroundeth all things in knowledge.

quran-a-barrier-until-the-day.text: That I may do right in that which I have left behind! But nay! It is but a word that he speaketh; and behind them is a barrier until the day when they are raised.
